newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Suicide bomber kills three in Tel Aviv cafe.
newsitem.headline: Suicide bomber kills three in Tel Aviv cafe.

text.p: A Palestinian Moslem suicide bomber killed three people in a crowded cafe in Tel Aviv on Friday, dealing a blow to faltering Middle East peacemaking.
The blast ripped through the outdoor terrace where families were relaxing at lunchtime ahead of the Jewish Sabbath holiday.
Half-finished meals lay on the few wooden tables that escaped the full force of the explosion at the Apropos cafe on central Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Street.
The attack came amid heightened Israeli-Palestinian tension over the groundbreaking on Tuesday of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Police initially said three people were killed, including the bomber. They later said one of the 43 people wounded died in hospital, raising the death toll to four.
An anonymous telephone caller told police the Hamas Islamic fundamentalist group carried out the attack.
Israel army radio said the bomber was a 28-year-old Palestinian from the Israeli-controlled West Bank village of Sourif.
The Israeli army imposed a curfew on Sourif and Palestinians said arrests were made.
A Hamas leader freed by the Palestinian Authority last week in Gaza said after the attack that only bombs could stop Israel's settlement drive.
At the cafe, an Israeli policewoman cradled a baby girl in her arms, looking for the crying infant's parents. The baby wore the tatters of a clown costume for the Jewish Purim festival.
"I saw her mother," medic Pinni Melech told Israel Radio. "Her whole face was burned, without an ear and a mess."
Mother and child were taken to Tel Aviv's Ichilov hospital -- the baby to intensive care. The hospital would not comment on the mother's fate.

It was a scene reminiscent of Tel Aviv one year ago at Purim when a Hamas suicide bomber killed 13 people in a shopping mall. The blast also came just over a week after seven Israeli schoolgirls were shot dead at the Jordan River by a Jordanian soldier.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the explosion as a "terrorist incident". But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arafat's Palestinian Authority of indirectly giving a green light to attackers.
Israel radio said that Arafat telephoned Netanyahu on Friday evening and expressed his condolences.

"I said these organisations understood from the things that were said to them they had the approval of the Palestinian Authority...There is no doubt they acted on the basis of that understanding," he told reporters while visiting wounded in hospital.

He was referring to Islamic fundamentalist organisations such as Hamas which carried out suicide bombings last year in an attempt to torpedo the Palestinian self-rule agreement with Israel which it sees as a sellout of Palestinian rights.
Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani rejected Netanyahu's accusation that the Authority had sanctioned violence, pinning the blame on the Israeli leader's settlement policy.

"It's a shame that the Israeli prime minister lies in front of his people and holds President Arafat responsible," Kanafani told reporters. "The person ultimately responsible for this painful deed is Netanyahu himself, who did not listen to the advice of the international community."

Netanyahu did not say he would halt peace talks with the Palestinians, who have accused the right-wing Israeli leader of fomenting unrest by forging ahead with the settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim or Har Homa, southeast of Jerusalem.
Israeli security chiefs issued warnings of possible unrest on Friday, the traditional day for Moslem prayers, over Har Homa, but the army was on alert mainly in the West Bank.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy criticised the U.S. State Department, saying it dismissed intelligence information that Israeli officials had relayed to their U.S. counterparts about a possible suicide attack.
Levy told Israel Channel One Television that he wrote "a strong letter" on Thursday to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright over the "amateurish" way the matter was handled.

Netanyahu clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the bombing, preventing Palestinian workers entering Israel. But hundreds of Palestinian youths clashed with Israeli soldiers in Hebron.
In Gaza, Palestinian police turned away buses carrying men to a Hamas rally in Khan Younis after the attack but the gathering went ahead.

"We must have the control and the power to stop the bulldozers of the enemy -- and our unarmed people will not prevent it but the holy warriors carrying explosives on their shoulders and exploding the enemies of God," Hamas leader Ibrahim al-Makadmeh told the crowd, estimated by reporters at 10,000.

Arafat released Makadmeh from jail this week to Israeli protests. He was imprisoned as part of crackdown on Hamas and Islamic Jihad after a wave of suicide attacks that killed 59 people in Israel last year.
In Damascus, a radical Palestinian group said Netanyahu should expect more attacks by Palestinians.
In Helsinki, U.S. President Bill Clinton, after a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, condemned the attack and said violence had no place in the Middle East peace process.
"I condemn it...," Clinton told a news conference. "There is no place for such acts of terror and violence in the peace process."
